Photograph: Vkontakte Russia The ‘ordinary’ woman accused of assassinating a Russian commander in Crimea Friends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan through Pjotr Sauer Sun 23 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It was just after dawn in Sevastopol when a powerful explosion tore through a quiet square in a residential district of the Russian-occupied Crimean port city. Hidden inside a rubbish bin, a bomb containing the equivalent of about 500g of TNT detonated on 13 August as Robert Shageev, the deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea fleet submarine brigade, walked past in naval uniform. He was killed on the spot. Within hours, investigators had a suspect. Police detained Margarita Reutt, a 32-year-old resident of Sochi, the Russian resort city about 300 miles across the Black Sea from Sevastopol. During a search, investigators said they had found a remote control they believed was used to detonate the bomb that killed Shageev, a former commander of Ukraine’s only submarine who switched allegiance to Russia in 2014 when Moscow annexed Crimea. According to the security service, she confessed to the attack and said that a handler linked to Ukrainian intelligence had promised her a large payment in cryptocurrency and documents that would allow her to leave Russia afterwards. View image in fullscreen Friends remember Margarita Reutt as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk. Photograph: Vkontakte The FSB also said Reutt showed no remorse. Those assertions could not be independently verified, and Russian security agencies have previously publicised purported confessions from detainees before their cases have reached court. But several people previously accused by Russia of carrying out similar attacks against military figures were later found by reporters to have been involved in the operations Moscow had accused them of conducting. What exactly drove Reutt to allegedly embark on such an audacious mission remains unclear. As with other cases involving accused Ukrainian intelligence operations, her trial is likely to take place behind closed doors, offering little opportunity for her to give her own account publicly. But interviews with a dozen friends and acquaintances, combined with an examination of years of her social media activity, offer a portrait of a determined and adventurous woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have hardened gradually, with signs of a more striking change emerging in the months leading up to the attack. “Rita believed that the country was going in the wrong direction,” said a longtime friend, using the diminutive form of her name. “But I am still shocked she went so far,” the friend added. View image in fullscreen An examination of Margarita Reutt’s social media activity offers a portrait of a determined woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have gradually hardened. Photograph: Vkontakte Russia quickly accused Reutt of carrying out the attack on the orders of Ukrainian intelligence. Kyiv has not commented on the bombing or Reutt’s alleged role in it. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have been linked to a string of assassinations and attempted killings of senior Russian military officers whom Kyiv has accused of involvement in the invasion. Ukrainian officials have occasionally acknowledged involvement in such operations, but more often have remained silent. The attacks have involved an array of methods and recruits, from committed anti-Kremlin saboteurs to Russians promised large sums of money. In other cases, unsuspecting couriers and delivery workers have effectively been used as mules. Usually, little is known about those accused of carrying out such attacks or how they prepared for them. Some have managed to escape, or were never publicly identified by Russian authorities, while others were killed carrying out their operations. The swift capture and naming of Reutt, however, offers a rare opportunity to examine the journey of a Russian citizen accused of turning against her own country. Reutt, born Margarita Yakovleva, grew up in Yaroslavl, a city north-east of Moscow, where she took the surname of the grandmother who largely raised her after her parents divorced. Friends recalled a largely unremarkable childhood, remembering her as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk. “Margarita was fearless. She would climb trees, jump off cars, do things most boys were scared of,” recalled one friend from her childhood. That streak followed her to Novosibirsk, thousands of miles to the east, where she studied management and threw herself into university life. Reutt became a regular at a local parachuting club, with photographs showing her jumping from Soviet-era aircraft, often the only woman among groups of men in camouflage gear. She also won prizes in amateur go-karting competitions and took up water polo, becoming goalkeeper for the university team and quickly distinguishing herself despite being new to the sport. “Margarita was so talented and never afraid of the ball,” recalled her water polo coach at the time. There was little then to suggest hostility towards the Kremlin. In Novosibirsk, Reutt became a well-liked member of a patriotic volunteer group that searched for the remains of Soviet soldiers killed during the second world war, part of a nationwide movement dedicated to recovering and reburying the war dead. After graduating, Reutt moved south to Sochi, the Black Sea resort that became her home. She briefly tried her hand at running a travel agency before joining Vitauct in the early 2020s, an alternative medicine company specialising in longevity. “She was the most ordinary person,” said Gennadiy Garbuzov, the company’s founder, who struggled to reconcile the woman he knew with the allegations now facing her. “There was nothing to indicate she would do this. She must have fallen under someone’s influence.” On the surface, her online life was similarly unremarkable. She posted frequently about health and animal rights and took to Telegram forums to discuss alternative medicine. Reutt also travelled widely. Leaked records from travel databases seen by the Guardian and photographs posted online show frequent trips abroad, including to Turkey, Thailand and Sri Lanka, where she often shared photographs of herself in bikinis at beach resorts. View image in fullscreen Margarita Reutt on one of her frequent trips abroad in a picture shared online. Photograph: Vkontakte “Margarita just seemed to be living her life and had lots of plans for the future,” said another colleague at Vitauct. “She was good-looking and popular,” the colleague added. In October 2025, Reutt travelled to Minsk for her sister’s wedding. Photographs from the celebration show her smiling among relatives and catching the bridal bouquet. To one friend she painted an idyllic picture of her life in Sochi, traversing mountains, waterfalls and canyons. “You can explore endlessly here, everything is lush and green,” she wrote to the friend. But beneath that outwardly happy life, another side of Reutt was becoming visible. She increasingly expressed concerns about environmental problems plaguing Sochi, and started to become involved in local volunteer initiatives, friends said. After a large oil spill in the Black Sea in December 2024, when two Russian tankers were wrecked in a storm, Reutt travelled to Anapa to join volunteers cleaning mazut, a heavy fuel oil, from contaminated beaches. Exactly when dissatisfaction with her surroundings hardened into something more political is difficult to establish. Friends described a growing estrangement from Russia that deepened after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “The war came as a shock,” said one friend, who recalled Reutt becoming increasingly outspoken in public about the fighting in Ukraine. “I told her once to keep quiet, otherwise she would get us both into trouble,” the friend said. By July 2025, her anti-war feelings had spilt into public view. While travelling on a Samara-Adler train, Reutt was fined under Russia’s sweeping law against “discrediting” the armed forces after reportedly shouting “Serves you right, Russians!” when news broke of a Ukrainian drone strike on a railway station in the Rostov region. The following February, Reutt posted the results of a genetic test showing she was 98% Russian, adding a hashtag declaring that she was “ashamed to be Russian”. Yet to friends and acquaintances, Reutt appeared to carry on much as before. She picked up occasional jobs, appeared in video clips made by friends and continued to travel. As recently as March, photographs from a trip to Cuba showed her drinking from a coconut. View image in fullscreen Margarita Reutt on a beach in Cuba. Photograph: Vkontakte It was only in late spring, several people who knew her said, that her behaviour began to change in ways they struggled to understand at the time. “She became more withdrawn,” recalled one friend. Around the same time, a group of friends began planning a trip together for the autumn. Reutt declined to join them without much explanation – an unusual response from someone friends said could be counted on to say yes to a new adventure. Another friend remembered Reutt suddenly acquiring a second phone. “She bought this second phone in the spring. She explained that she needed it for work, but it didn’t really make sense to me at the time.” “Margarita was hiding something,” the friend added. “I thought maybe she had a new boyfriend.” By the summer, Reutt had begun spending more time in Crimea, the place where she would eventually be arrested. One acquaintance said she explained the trips to Crimea by saying she was scouting possible locations for video shoots, having recently begun appearing more frequently in music clips. What she was actually doing in Crimea – and when, if at all, she came into contact with Ukrainian intelligence – remains unknown. If Russia’s allegations that she was recruited by Ukraine are true, Reutt would join a growing group of Russian citizens accused of being enlisted by Ukrainian intelligence to carry out sabotage and assassinations deep behind the frontlines. Such recruits offer obvious advantages: they can move around Russia more freely, and attract less scrutiny than Ukrainian operatives, and they can reach targets far from the frontline without putting trained agents at risk. Women have featured prominently in several of the most high-profile operations, potentially attracting even less suspicion. For those close to Reutt, there is no easy explanation for how the woman they remember ended up accused of carrying out an assassination. But a friend of two decades recalled a stubborn determination to follow through on whatever she decided to do. “If she had a plan in mind, she would do it,” the friend said. “Even if it was something like this.” Explore more on these topics Russia Crimea Ukraine Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.miragenews.com/wzl-1-boeing-.text: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Travel 12 Aug 2026 2:24 am AEST Date Time Share Wojskowe Zakłady Lotnicze Nr 1 S.A. (WZL-1), the Military Central Bureau of Design and Technology S.A. (WCKBT) and Boeing have signed offset implementation agreements to establish long-term industrial cooperation supporting the sustainment, maintenance and ground support of Poland's AH-64E Apache helicopter fleet. The signing ceremony took place at the WZL-1 facility in Łódź, with representatives from the Polish Ministry of National Defence, the Government of the Republic of Poland, and the Polish Armed Forces in attendance. Under the agreements, Boeing will support WZL-1 as they start to support the AH-64E aircraft for the Polish Armed Forces. The center will provide maintenance, repair, and overhaul services, including organizational- and intermediate-level inspections and repairs, as well as selected depot-level component repairs. Boeing and WCBKT will evaluate selected WCBKT ground support equipment for use with the AH-64E Apache helicopter. This effort will assess the feasibility of Polish engineering solutions in support of the combat helicopters and help inform their future role in the Apache sustainment program. "Signing these agreements marks a significant milestone in Boeing's partnership with Poland and demonstrates our enduring commitment to supporting the Polish Armed Forces through robust, in-country sustainment and maintenance capabilities," said Marc-Olivier Sabourin, Vice-President EICLA & Training Solutions, Boeing Global Services. "Together with WZL-1 and WCKBT, we are building the industrial framework, technical expertise and workforce needed to support Poland's Apache fleet for decades, while strengthening Poland's sovereign defense capabilities." As part of offset implementation agreements, Boeing will leverage its sustainment expertise to deliver technical insight, resources, and training to WZL-1 and WCKBT's highly skilled workforce, which will enable continuous modernization and operational readiness of the Apache platform within Poland. "For WZL-1, establishing the largest Apache support infrastructure in Europe is both a responsibility and a natural extension of our core business activities. This agreement will enable us to provide support to the Polish Armed Forces, significantly enhancing their operational capabilities," said Jacek A. Goszczyński, PhD Eng., CEO of Military Aviation Works No. 1 S.A. (WZL-1). "Signing the implementation agreement with Boeing marks a significant step toward increasing the Polish defense industry's participation in the AH-64E Apache support program. For WCBKT S.A., this represents an opportunity to further develop capabilities and strengthen the company's position as a national center of expertise in the design, manufacture, and servicing of ground support equipment for modern military platforms. We believe that utilizing equipment developed and manufactured by WCBKT S.A.-alongside the potential of the Polish industry-will enhance logistical support efficiency and strengthen the operational independence of the Polish Armed Forces. We are confident that WCBKT S.A.'s expertise and the quality of our solutions will enable us to effectively support AH-64E Apache operations with state-of-the-art ground support equipment." said Roman Fiszer, PhD Eng., CEO of WCBKT S.A. Poland has contracted for 96 AH-64E Apache helicopters. Poland's offset agreements support the implementation of its AH-64E Apache program by developing critical maintenance and sustainment capabilities domestically. Currently the 19 th nation operating the Apache, Poland will become the world's second-largest Apache operator after the United States with the addition of its AH-64E fleet. Proven in combat, the Apache continues to demonstrate its ability to adapt to missions such as Counter-UAS and absorb new technologies to remain dominant against evolving global threats. Approximately 1,300 Apache helicopters are in operation worldwide. /Public Release. https://greentechlead.com/renewable-ener.text: Home Solar Wind Power E Vehicle Climate Renewable Energy Water Home Solar Wind Power E Vehicle Climate Renewable Energy Water Renewable Energy CIP Raises $3 bn for GMF II, Advances Battery, Solar and Wind Projects in Chile, Mexico and Romania August 14, 2026 By Editor CIP Share Copy URL Linkedin X Facebook Email Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has completed fundraising for its second Growth Markets Fund , securing approximately $3 billion in commitments to finance large-scale renewable energy and power infrastructure across 15 high-growth, middle-income markets in Eastern Europe, Asia and Latin America. Growth Markets Fund II (GMF II), including associated investment vehicles, is nearly three times the size of CIP’s first Growth Markets Fund. At final close, the fund’s total value exceeded paid-in capital, while $1.6 billion had already been committed across nine investments. CIP expects GMF II to be fully committed within one to two years, supported by a visible pipeline of solar, wind, battery storage and grid-related projects. GMF II Attracts Global Institutional Investors GMF II received commitments from sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, development finance institutions, impact-focused family offices and returning investors. The fundraising expanded CIP’s institutional investor base across Asia, the Middle East and North America. The fund focuses on developing and constructing greenfield energy infrastructure in countries where increasing electricity consumption, grid constraints and energy-security requirements are creating demand for new generation and storage capacity. CIP’s first Growth Markets Fund provides an operating blueprint for the new strategy. GMF I is expected to deliver approximately 8.7 GW of critical energy infrastructure across more than 50 projects in India and South Africa. Patache Battery Project Enters Construction in Chile GMF II has issued Final Notice to Proceed for the 300 MW/1,500 MWh Patache battery energy storage project in Chile. The decision authorises construction under the project’s principal supply and construction agreements. Patache will provide five hours of storage capacity and is located near high-quality solar resources, existing transmission infrastructure and energy-intensive industrial clusters. It will store surplus solar electricity produced during daytime hours and discharge it when power demand is higher. The project is designed to reduce peak-hour dependence on thermal generation, lower carbon dioxide emissions and support the integration of additional utility-scale solar power into Chile’s electricity system. Patache has also qualified for an internationally recognised carbon-offset programme. GMF II is developing the project alongside co-investors holding a minority interest. Patache follows CIP’s Arena battery energy storage project in northern Chile’s Antofagasta region. The 220 MW/1,100 MWh Arena facility has completed construction and is supplying electricity to the grid. CIP said Arena was constructed below budget and is the largest standalone battery project commissioned in Chile. La Esperanza Solar Secures $510 Million Financing in Mexico CIP has also reached final investment decision and financial close for La Esperanza Solar in Campeche on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. It is the first CIP investment in Mexico to reach financial close. The project combines 420 MWdc of solar photovoltaic capacity with a 150 MW battery system capable of operating for five hours. Its total storage capacity will be 750 MWh, making it one of Mexico’s largest battery energy storage systems. Construction is underway, with commercial operations scheduled for 2028. The facility will add generation and storage capacity to the Yucatán Peninsula, where increasing electricity demand has intensified the need for a more reliable and flexible power system. The battery system will store renewable electricity and deliver it when required, improving grid stability and the availability of clean power outside peak solar-production periods. La Esperanza Solar has secured approximately $510 million in debt facilities from five international and regional commercial banks: BNP Paribas, JPMorgan Chase Bank, Natixis CIB, Santander and Scotiabank. Equity is being provided by GMF II, with an expected co-investment from Mexican retirement-fund administrator Profuturo. The project forms part of CIP’s broader expansion in Mexico, where the company has started construction on the country’s first large-scale solar-and-battery projects after securing the largest capacity allocation under the government’s recent binding planning framework. Pestera II Wind Farm Reaches Financial Close in Romania In Romania, GMF II has completed financial close for the 392 MW Pestera II onshore wind project in Constanța County. CIP describes it as one of Romania’s largest investments in new renewable energy infrastructure and one of the largest project-finance transactions completed in Central and Eastern Europe. Pestera II secured a 15-year contract for difference covering 245 MW of its capacity in December 2024. Commercial operations are expected to begin in 2028. The wind farm is intended to improve Romania’s security of electricity supply while providing competitively priced renewable power under a long-term revenue framework. Project financing includes approximately €510 million in facilities supplied by a consortium of seven local and international banks: Erste Bank and Banca Comerciala Romana, Deutsche Bank, Societe Generale and BRD, Eurobank, and Piraeus Bank. Equity is being contributed by GMF II and two co-investors—the European Investment Bank and a Danish pension fund. Nordex will supply 56 N163-6.X wind turbines, each rated at 7.0 MW. Electrogrup will serve as the balance-of-plant contractor, while Blue Power Partners will provide construction-management services. CIP Builds Growth-Market Renewable Energy Pipeline The Chilean, Mexican and Romanian projects demonstrate GMF II’s emphasis on utility-scale infrastructure that combines renewable generation, energy storage and grid-support capabilities. With around $3 billion raised, $1.6 billion already allocated to nine investments and full commitment expected within one to two years, CIP is positioning GMF II as a major source of capital for renewable energy expansion across its 15 target markets. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/02/chri.text: A condemned female murderer who survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee is in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care," her lawyer said on Thursday.In an extraordinary chain of events, Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital on Wednesday night, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital."What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care," Randy Spivey said in a virtual news conference on Thursday afternoon, declining to provide further details.He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike's death sentence."After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now."Experts on the US death penalty said the case was unprecedented."This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre.The centre counts seven inmates whose executions could not be carried out because medical staff were unable to establish IV lines, but "Pike is the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."Late on Thursday, US President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike's could fail, telling reporters that it "shouldn't be very difficult."'Loudly snoring'The case had already attracted scrutiny as Pike would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.Kim Chandler, a media witness with the Associated Press, told CBS News that "Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began" at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville."A couple of times she looked around the room. At one point she looked towards prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way," Chandler said.Pike later began snoring and witnesses listened from the viewing area for about an hour before being ushered out.The condemned woman was "loudly snoring, clearly very alive" as journalists left, Chandler told CBS.Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition."I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt" to start an IV line, Spivey said.Lawyer Stephen Ferrell said medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike's arm instead of the bloodstream."It sounds like that is likely to have occurred," he said.Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff her arm felt like it would "burst open," and Spivey said he saw her right arm turn purple, especially after the second lethal injection.Pike had not been scared to die, Ferrell said."It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that's what happened, minus the death."'A mess'The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol," adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an "off-site medical facility."Governor Lee called for a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed execution.The state's remaining scheduled execution, convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton is scheduled to die on 3 December, would not be carried out this year, Lee added.Pike's case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp.The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told NBC News the botched execution was "a mess."Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.Following a flurry of legal filings that delayed the execution by several hours, the US Supreme Court on Wednesday night cleared the way for the punishment to go ahead.In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike."The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," his office said on X.Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
